newsitem.title: TOGO: World transport union focuses on Africa air safety.
newsitem.headline: World transport union focuses on Africa air safety.

text.p: International transport union leaders opened talks in Togo on Tuesday, with delegates seeking tighter air safety controls in Africa following a string of air disasters on the continent.

Organisers said the meeting of the International Transport Federation (ITF), which ends on Thursday, would focus on how to regulate the air transport industry which is going through extensive deregulation.

"This crisis is due to globalisation of civil aviation which in Africa has meant privatisation of companies and deregulation," ITF Francophone country coordinator Nazinigouba Kabore told Reuters before talks opened.

The ITF, meeting in Lome for its sixth two-yearly African Regional Civil Aviation Conference, says it will address a "crisis" faced by Africa's air transport sector after crashes, strikes and increasing airline debts.
The International Federation of Airline Pilots' Associations (IFALPA) slammed air safety in Africa at a meeting in November.
It panned Africa as a disaster area, where collisions were only avoided by the skill of pilots, and awarded the continent an IFALPA "Black Star" high-risk rating.

ITF's London world headquarters spokesman Richard Flint said about 40 union bodies from 30 African countries would aim to agree on a union strategy for Africa and build up cooperation with African intergovernmental aviation organisations.
"There is a spread of liberalisation (worldwide) and what people call open skies. We believe this is having a detrimental effect on safety," he told Reuters by telephone from London.
IFALPA statistics show Africa has a crash rate of 14.9 per million flights, against 9.4 in South America, 1.3 in Asia and 0.7 in Europe and North America.

"At least 75 percent of the air traffic infrastructure in Africa is unable to provide the services that are required for the safe and expeditious operation of flights through their area of responsibility," IFALPA said at the time.
The ITF has launched a campaign against airline deregulation following its maritime sector campaign against ships using flags of convenience.
"The ITF is leading a campaign against open skies and insists that, while liberalisation goes ahead, the interests of passengers and users are taken ito account," said Kabore.
Crashes are not rare in Africa. A charter flight crash in Senegal on February 1 killing 23 passengers was the latest.
A Boeing 727 crashed into a Nigerian lagoon killing all 142 people on board in November. Nigerian officals afterwards acknowledged three major crashes in Nigeria in 1996.
In January 1996, a cargo plane crashed on takeoff in Zaire killing 300 people in a crowded Kinshasa market.
